title: ConcurrentDictionary traps and immutability
summary: Why GetOrAdd can run your factory twice, the Lazy<Task<T>> fix for caches, compound operations that are not atomic, and immutable snapshots for read-mostly data.

steps.title: Each call is atomic; your sequence of calls is not
body: `ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>` makes every **single** operation thread-safe: `TryAdd`, `TryGetValue`, `TryRemove`, `TryUpdate`,
`GetOrAdd`, `AddOrUpdate`. It does **not** make two calls in a row atomic, and it does **not** run your delegates under its lock.
`GetOrAdd(key, factory)` looks up the key; if it is missing it calls `factory` **outside** any lock, then tries to add the result. Two
threads that miss at the same time **both run the factory**; one value is stored and both callers get that one, but the other
factory's work (a connection opened, an HTTP call made) is wasted or leaked.
The card runs `GetOrAdd` for real on two threads. The factory counts its calls with `Interlocked`. Find an interleaving where
`created` is 2, or press **Try every interleaving**.

steps.prompt: Each line runs on many threads against one shared `ConcurrentDictionary<string, int> stock`. Atomic, or a race?
items: `if (stock.TryGetValue("A1", out var n)) stock.TryUpdate("A1", n - 1, n);` (checking the result)
explain: `AddOrUpdate` retries its update delegate until its compare-and-swap succeeds, so the *result* is atomic (the delegate may run more
than once: keep it pure). `TryUpdate(key, new, expected)` is a compare-and-swap; it is correct when you check its result and retry.
A read followed by a separate write is a race, however safe each call is.

steps.title: Lazy<Task<T>>: one factory call per key
body: Store a **`Lazy<Task<T>>`** instead of the value. Creating a `Lazy` is cheap and has no side effects, so it does not matter if two
threads create one each: only the stored `Lazy` is ever *started*, and every caller awaits the same task.
```csharp fragment
readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<Task<Conn>>> _conns = new();
public async Task<Conn> GetAsync(string host)
var lazy = _conns.GetOrAdd(host, h => new Lazy<Task<Conn>>(() => _open(h)));
try { return await lazy.Value; }
catch
_conns.TryRemove(KeyValuePair.Create(host, lazy));   // do not cache a failure forever
throw;
The `TryRemove(KeyValuePair)` overload removes the entry **only if** it is still that same `Lazy`, so a retry that already replaced
it is not thrown away.

steps.explain: `TryAdd` never overwrites. `TryUpdate(key, newValue, comparisonValue)` is a compare-and-swap: it writes only when the current value equals the comparison value (1 here, not 2).

steps.title: Immutability: share it, never change it
body: The safest shared state is state nobody can modify. For **read-mostly** data (configuration, routing tables, price lists, feature
flags), build a new immutable object and swap the reference:
```csharp fragment
private FrozenDictionary<string, Route> _routes = FrozenDictionary<string, Route>.Empty;
public Route? Find(string path) => Volatile.Read(ref _routes).GetValueOrDefault(path);   // readers: no lock
public void Reload(IEnumerable<Route> routes) =>                                        // writers: build, then swap
Volatile.Write(ref _routes, routes.ToFrozenDictionary(r => r.Path));
Readers always see a complete, consistent table, never a half-updated one. With several writers, use `ImmutableInterlocked.Update`
(a CAS loop for you). Records with `init` properties and `with` expressions make immutable domain objects cheap to write.

steps.prompt: A pricing service reads its price table on every request (thousands per second) and reloads it every five minutes. Which design fits best?
options: Build a new `FrozenDictionary` on reload and swap the reference; readers use whatever reference they read
A `Dictionary` protected by a `lock` taken on every read
A `ConcurrentDictionary` that the reload clears and refills key by key
A `ReaderWriterLockSlim` held for the whole reload
steps.explain: Reads take no lock and always see one complete table. Clearing and refilling a shared dictionary lets readers see an empty or half-filled table mid-reload.

steps.title: A connection cache that opens each host once
prompt: Write a class **`ConnectionCache`** with a constructor `ConnectionCache(Func<string, Task<Conn>> open)` and
- concurrent callers for the same host share **one** call to `open` and get the **same** `Conn`;
- if `open` fails, the caller gets the exception and the **next** call tries again (the failure is not cached).
Write the dictionary type in full, `System.Collections.Concurrent.ConcurrentDictionary<...>` (this editor has no `using` line).
The tests hold `open`'s answer until both callers are waiting, so a version that can open twice is caught every time.
starter: if (_conns.TryGetValue(host, out var conn)) return conn;
solution: var lazy = _conns.GetOrAdd(host, h => new Lazy<Task<Conn>>(() => open(h)));
template: Dojo.Eq("Two concurrent callers open db1 once", 1, dojoOpens);
Dojo.Check("Both callers get the same connection", ReferenceEquals(dojoConnA, dojoConnB), "They got different Conn objects.");
await Dojo.ThrowsAsync<IOException>("A failed open reaches the caller", () => dojoCache.GetAsync("bad"));
await Dojo.ThrowsAsync<IOException>("The next call tries again", () => dojoCache.GetAsync("bad"));
Dojo.Eq("The failure was not cached: open ran again", 3, dojoOpens);
hints: Store `Lazy<Task<Conn>>` in the dictionary and await `lazy.Value`.
Wrap the await in try/catch; in the catch, `_conns.TryRemove(KeyValuePair.Create(host, lazy));` then `throw;`.
explain: Notice the test: both callers start before `open` is allowed to finish. That *forces* the dangerous interleaving instead of hoping
for it, and it is how you should write tests for your own caches. `HybridCache` (Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid) gives you
the same stampede protection out of the box, plus expiry and a distributed second level.
